q2.answer: The resume position is `build_cursor` (the id of the last saved product) in the single-row `sync_state` table in SQLite. Each page's rows and the cursor update are written in one SQLite transaction, so they commit together or not at all.

q3.answer: Before page 1 the client reads a watermark W (the highest committed change_seq) from `/sync/watermark` and commits it as `build_watermark`. After the last page it replays `/changes?since=W` (catch-up). Because change_seq is assigned at commit and rows become visible in order, every change after W is returned by the replay, and applying changes is idempotent.

q5.answer: A new generation is built beside the active one in the same `products` table, keyed by `(generation, id)`. It follows the same steps as a first download: watermark, pages, catch-up. The old catalogue stays visible and untouched. In one transaction, step 9 sets `active_generation = build_generation` and clears the build fields. That happens only after catch-up is complete. The old generation's rows are then deleted in the background.

q9.answer: Each incoming record is applied as an upsert (or delete, for a tombstone) keyed by id. It is applied only if its change_seq is at least the stored row's change_seq. Lower ones are skipped.

q10.answer: The start position is `change_cursor_active`, which holds the active generation's last applied change_seq. It is seeded from `change_cursor_build` at promotion (step 9), which itself starts at the build watermark. The cursor moves forward to the response's `last_seq` in the same transaction that applies each response's changes. If a run stops partway, the cursor stays at the last saved response.

q11.answer: The change feed reads the Postgres products table, filtering on `change_seq > since` and ordered by `change_seq` ascending, using an index on change_seq. A stored `purge_floor` is also read to decide whether to return 410. Deletes are the soft-delete tombstone rows, which appear as `{id, change_seq, deleted: true}`.
